I wanted to see too [?]
                    John
1942-07-02_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Added later in a different hand, probably by Tom's brother John, who visited him in New York in July 1942.

1942-07-06_tom-to-mother.txt.text: Our bounds are from 110th St. to 122nd St.
The floors are decks, stairs - ladders

1942-07-06_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The Fourth of July. For the midshipmen it was a normal day of drill, a parade and a USO show (see the next letter).

1942-07-11_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom's brother John was visiting New York.

1942-07-18_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Dick and Betty married about July 18, 1942.

1942-07-18_tom-to-mother.txt.text: Please don't say much about what I tell you the school
1942-07-18_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Wartime security. Posters warned 'Loose lips might sink ships', and officer candidates were told not to discuss their training.

1942-07-20_tom-to-mother.txt.note: About 900 men entered with Tom in July 1942; 753 were commissioned in October.

1942-07-23_tom-to-mother.txt.note: A newspaper write-up of Dick and Betty's wedding (see July 18).

1942-07-27_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The fellow from Indiana, Pa., whom Tom met on the train (see July 6).

1942-08-05_tom-to-mother.txt.note: After deductions (insurance, uniforms, etc.) Tom's first pay was $4.70, about $90 in today's money.

1942-08-18_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Almost certainly the Dieppe Raid of Aug. 19, 1942, so this letter was probably finished on the 19th despite its date.

1942-08-22_tom-to-mother-postcard.txt.text: I am having some proofs sent home
1942-08-22_tom-to-mother-postcard.txt.note: Proofs of the formal portrait Tom had taken during a short liberty about Aug. 13 (see Aug. 10 and Sept. 17), probably the uniform photo later used with his commissioning announcement.

1942-08-27_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Notre Dame ran a V-7 indoctrination school from 1942; some of its graduates came to Columbia for the midshipman course.

1942-08-27_tom-to-mother.txt.text: Furnald who I knew at State

1942-08-27_tom-to-mother.txt.note: A member of Beta Theta Pi fraternity. 'But a good fellow' suggests a friendly rivalry with Tom's own fraternity at Penn State.

1942-09-01_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Mother's birthday was in late August.
A period joke comparing the instructors to residents of Polk State School, an institution for people with intellectual disabilities. Kept as written.

1942-09-01_tom-to-mother.txt.text: We get a cruise on Thursday
1942-09-01_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Practical seamanship training aboard small vessels in New York harbor.

1942-09-09_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom wrote 'August' by mistake: the content (Labor Day, finals on the 15th) shows this is Sept. 9, 1942.
The family had a lake cottage where they spent holidays; Tom mentions 'the cottage' again in 1943.
Tom means Oct. 21, the date that was finally used.

1942-09-09_tom-to-mother.txt.text: any Jew could get permission to go home for their holidays
1942-09-09_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom records antisemitic feeling among the midshipmen. Antisemitism was widespread and openly expressed in 1940s America, including in the officer corps, even as the country fought Nazi Germany. Kept as written as part of the historical record.

1942-09-09_tom-to-mother.txt.text: My roommate was caught in the last bilge

1942-09-26_tom-to-mother.txt.note: A classroom exercise in dead reckoning and celestial navigation. Tom used these skills for real on LCI(L)-62's Pacific crossing five months later.
A small deck gun (3-inch bore) mounted on escorts and auxiliaries; LCIs themselves carried 20mm guns.

1942-09-29_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Navy diesel engineering schools trained officers for the diesel-powered landing craft, subchasers and submarines.

1942-10-09_tom-to-mother.txt.note: A formal parade review by a flag officer before graduation.

1942-10-21_newspaper-clipping-commission.text: Mr. and Mrs. John A. Beck

his new post, which was
not revealed
1942-10-21_newspaper-clipping-commission.note: Wartime censorship: newspapers did not print where servicemen were posted. Tom was headed for the Amphibious Force at Norfolk.

1942-11-01_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Overnight passenger steamers still ran on Chesapeake Bay between Baltimore or Washington and Norfolk.

1942-11-04_tom-to-mother-norfolk.txt.note: Solomons was built in a hurry in 1942; many buildings were temporary huts, and the base was known for its mud.
A Commerce & Finance graduate, probably Tom's Penn State major, as opposed to an engineer.

1942-11-09_tom-to-mother-monday.txt.note: British Commandos and the new U.S. Army Rangers were celebrated in the 1942 press, and the idea of amphibious 'commando' work had a romantic appeal.
Southern Maryland was known for its (legal in some counties) slot machines from the 1940s to the 1960s.
A racial slur for the Black pianist. It was common in white speech of the period and is kept as written as part of the historical record.

1942-11-16_tom-to-mother-and-dad.txt.note: A point near the Solomons base on the Patuxent River or Chesapeake Bay used as a training mark; the exact location is not confirmed.

1942-11-18_tom-to-dad.txt.note: Betty and 'the Johns' visited Tom at Solomons on Saturday, Nov. 21 (see the Nov. 22 letters).

1942-11-18_tom-to-dad.txt.text: Yanks are doing allright in Africa

1942-11-18_tom-to-dad.txt.note: Dad had been seriously ill in November 1942.

1942-11-20_tom-to-dad.txt.note: Mother's letter apparently reported how seriously ill Dad had been.

1942-11-22_tom-to-dad-sunday.txt.note: The visit of Saturday, Nov. 21, 1942, also described in the letter to 'Sis' written the same day.

1942-11-22_tom-to-sis-betty-undated.txt.text: Tell the kid I said hello
1942-11-22_tom-to-sis-betty-undated.txt.note: Perhaps Betty's child or a younger family member (possibly 'Hickory').

1942-11-24_tom-to-dad.txt.text: like a pig pen when it rains

1942-11-26_tom-to-dad-thanksgiving.txt.text: some one type of people seem to get soft jobs
1942-11-26_tom-to-dad-thanksgiving.txt.note: An antisemitic remark (made explicit a few lines later), echoing Dad's letter. The charge that Jews avoided hard or dangerous service was a common prejudice of the time, and false: about 550,000 Jewish Americans served in WWII. Kept as written.
Antisemitic remark, kept as written as part of the historical record.

1942-11-28_tom-to-dad-and-mother.txt.text: Solomons and in a few other skirmishes
1942-11-28_tom-to-dad-and-mother.txt.note: Here 'Solomons' means the Solomon Islands (Guadalcanal), not the Maryland base.
Tom singles out a roommate's religion; given the antisemitic remarks in nearby letters, it reads as a prejudiced aside. Kept as written.
Time, Nov. 30, 1942. The article on page 70 is not identified.

1942-11-xx_tom-to-mother-wednesday.txt.text: all the soft jobs are going to the Jews
1942-11-xx_tom-to-mother-wednesday.txt.note: Antisemitic and anti-Japanese remarks, common prejudices of the time. 'Jap' was the standard wartime slur for Japanese people. Kept as written as part of the historical record.
New LCIs built at Gulf Coast yards trained in the Gulf of Mexico before deploying.

1942-12-03_tom-to-mother-and-dad.txt.text: Hank & Harriet - a pair of sox

1942-12-03_tom-to-mother-and-dad.txt.note: Dirt roads were sprayed with oil to keep down dust and mud, a familiar practice in the Pennsylvania oil country too.
Tom arrived at Solomons on Nov. 5, 1942, about a month earlier.

1942-12-05_tom-to-mother-and-dad.txt.text: (I am the censor for my crew)

1942-12-10_tom-to-folks.txt.note: Tom's crew was aboard the training ship LCI(L)-218 in the Chesapeake/Norfolk area.

1942-12-14_tom-to-mother-and-dad.txt.text: The topics we aren't allowed to write about

1942-12-28_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom had been home to Karns City for Christmas 1942. It was probably the last time he saw his father.

1942-12-29_tom-to-mother.txt.text: not going into the heart of it
1942-12-29_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Most East Coast amphibious crews of this period went to North Africa. Tom was hinting (within censorship rules) that his crew was headed elsewhere: the Gulf, and then the Pacific.

1942-12-29_tom-to-mother.txt.text: likes the Chinks, but not the Japs
1942-12-29_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Ethnic slurs for Chinese and Japanese people, common in 1940s America. Kept as written.

1943-01-02_tom-to-mother.txt.text: officers club at the Navy Yard
1943-01-02_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The Norfolk Navy Yard, in Portsmouth, Va.

1943-01-05_tom-to-mother-houston.txt.text: The base here is small but very nice
1943-01-05_tom-to-mother-houston.txt.note: Probably the Navy facility serving the Brown Shipbuilding yard on Greens Bayou, Houston, where LCI(L)-345 was built.

1943-01-05_tom-to-mother-houston.txt.text:
there isn't a bar in the whole
state

1943-01-08_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
paper work connected with equiping a
ship
1943-01-08_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom's crew was fitting out LCI(L)-345, which was commissioned on Jan. 22.

1943-01-15_tom-to-mother.txt.text: Chet just came back from the Pacific Fleet
1943-01-15_tom-to-mother.txt.note: A wedding write-up exaggerated Chet's service; he was still in the East.

1943-01-15_tom-to-mother.txt.text: $21 as A.S., $195 as Midshipman, & $300 as Ensign
1943-01-15_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom's 1942 service pay by rank: Apprentice Seaman, Midshipman and Ensign. His whole 1942 Navy income of about $666 is roughly $13,000 today.

1943-01-18_tom-to-mother.txt.text: we are going to the southwest
1943-01-18_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom hints that his ship is bound for the Pacific. As it turned out, the LCIs went straight through the Panama Canal without stopping in California.

1943-01-24_tom-to-mother.txt.note: USS LCI(L)-345 was commissioned Friday, Jan. 22, 1943.
Mail went c/o Brown Shipbuilding, the yard that built LCI(L)-345.
Probably an oil or gas lease on family property, handled by brother John; the Becks were in the oil business.

1943-01-28_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom grew up in western Pennsylvania oil country, and his family was in the oil business.

1943-01-31_tom-to-mother.txt.text: The executive officer on another ship is sick

1943-01-31_tom-to-mother.txt.note: A wedding in Houston (name reading uncertain).

1943-02-03_tom-to-mother.txt.text: It happened this evening - I was transfered
1943-02-03_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom joined USS LCI(L)-62 as executive officer on Feb. 3, 1943. By his April 7 letter the ship sailed the next day.
A full lieutenant, two ranks above Tom. LCI skippers were usually ensigns or lieutenants (j.g.), so this was an experienced captain.

1943-02-11_tom-to-mother.txt.text: I came aboard this ship the night before sailing
we arrived here and are now at anchor
1943-02-11_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Censored location. About a week out from Texas, hot in February, and 'left the States': almost certainly the Panama Canal Zone, the route to the Pacific.

1943-02-11_tom-to-mother.txt.text: I never took a sextant sight before

1943-02-11_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The LCIs travelled in a group with a lead ship doing the main navigation.

1943-02-13_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
Almost every other door leads to a
bar
1943-02-13_tom-to-mother.txt.note: This fits Colón, Panama, at the Atlantic end of the Canal, notorious among sailors for its bars and nightlife.

1943-02-13_tom-to-mother.txt.text: they can take quite a bit of punishment
1943-02-13_tom-to-mother.txt.note: LCIs were flat-bottomed and rolled badly in open sea. Crews joked that they would 'roll on wet grass'.

1943-02-18_tom-to-mother-typed.txt.note: A joke about the old colonial courting custom of sharing a bed fully clothed (and bundled), here meaning 'keeping warm'.
Someone from home whose departure was apparently a story; not identified.

1943-02-22_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The next leg was the long Pacific crossing.
Tom realised the ship would not stop in California: it was going straight across the Pacific from Panama.

1943-02-23_tom-to-mother.txt.text: anchored out to-night and I think for the last time for quite sometime
Don't worry if you don't hear from me for a couple of months
1943-02-23_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Letters resumed from the South Pacific in mid-March, and the family got a reassuring cable on April 12.

1943-03-12_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Early March 1943, crossing from the Canal toward the South Pacific.

1943-03-12_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
close enough to an island yesterday that we could
see some mountains
1943-03-12_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Perhaps one of the high islands of French Polynesia (the Marquesas or Society Islands) on the approach to Bora Bora.
Powerful 'clear-channel' AM stations such as KVOO Tulsa or WKY Oklahoma City could be heard thousands of miles away at night.
About Mar. 18-19, after roughly three weeks at sea from Panama: probably Bora Bora in the Society Islands, the usual first stop.

1943-04-07_tom-to-unc.txt.text: The ship I was orginally assigned to
One of the other ships lost and officer so I replaced him

1943-04-07_tom-to-unc.txt.note: Banana beer or 'jungle juice', brewed on many Pacific islands.

1943-04-07_tom-to-unc.txt.text:
It
looks like a fair sized city from out here in the bay
1943-04-07_tom-to-unc.txt.note: Probably Nouméa, New Caledonia, the only real city on the route and the base where LCI Flotilla Five trained in spring 1943. Suva, Fiji is another possibility.

1943-04-07_tom-to-unc.txt.text:
the night I left Mother was the toughest day
I have had
1943-04-07_tom-to-unc.txt.note: One of several hints that Dad had died shortly before Tom went overseas.

1943-04-12_cablegram-tom-to-mother.txt.text: ALL WELL AND SAFE PLEASE DONT WORRY LOVE KISSES
1943-04-12_cablegram-tom-to-mother.txt.note: The family's first word from Tom in about two months. Cables were expensive and charged by the word, and a telegram at the door often meant bad news, which is why Tom later worried it scared her.

1943-04-13_tom-to-mother-vmail.txt.text: c/o P. M. San Francisco, Cal.

1943-04-13_tom-to-mother-vmail.txt.note: Probably an address on East Pearl Street, Butler, Pa., likely relatives.

1943-04-13_tom-to-mother-vmail.txt.text: it sounds good on all fronts
1943-04-13_tom-to-mother-vmail.txt.note: In mid-April 1943 the Allies were closing in on the Axis armies in Tunisia, and the Japanese had evacuated Guadalcanal in February.

1943-04-15_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
Mail Call for the
first time since we left the States
1943-04-15_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The first mail in about ten weeks: 35-40 letters and 4 packages at once.
Selective Service. In 1943 college men were being drafted, and George had to choose between waiting to be drafted and volunteering for a Navy program (he chose Navy V-12).
Employers kept 'honor rolls' of employees in the armed forces. Tom evidently worked for a company before the war, perhaps a family oil concern.
The past tense is one of the hints that Dad had died.
The stationery was embossed 'DEPARTMENT OF THE NAVY / U.S.S. LCI(L)-62'.

1943-04-21_tom-to-mother.txt.text: Most of the letters I censor

1943-04-21_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Air mail was sent on thin, lightweight paper to save weight.

1943-04-25_tom-to-mother-and-all.txt.note: Possibly an allusion to his father's recent death.
An unidentified address, possibly a property of Tom's; the joke about 'sending John around' is not explained.

1943-04-25_tom-to-mother-and-all.txt.text: Air-mail is the best service out here

1943-04-30_tom-to-mother-vmail.txt.text: [Morse-code-like dots and dashes typed at lower left]
1943-04-30_tom-to-mother-vmail.txt.note: Perhaps a playful sign-off in Morse code; not decoded.

1943-05-03_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Mail reached ships in forward areas irregularly, sometimes weeks of letters at once.

1943-05-09_tom-to-mother-mothersday.txt.note: This was Mother's Day, though Tom doesn't say so.
Crews at advanced bases were given occasional 'recreation parties' ashore with beer and ball games.

1943-05-11_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The Engineering Officer was wrong: V-12 was a college-based officer training program, not the WAVES.

1943-05-11_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
What picture of Dad are they going to use in the
school-house?
1943-05-11_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Apparently a memorial to Tom's father at the local school. This is one of the strongest hints that he had died.
The family's summer cottage at 'the Lake' (see Sept. 1942).
Two days after this letter, on May 13, the Axis forces in Tunisia surrendered.

1943-05-16_tom-to-mother.txt.text: John has made up his mind

1943-05-17_tom-to-mother.txt.text: personal clothing that we are sending home
1943-05-17_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Crews in the tropics were told to send home or store woollens, blues and whites they would not need.

1943-05-24_tom-to-mother.txt.note: A new port after another voyage, perhaps toward Espiritu Santo or the Guadalcanal area. LCI Flotilla Five moved up from Nouméa to the Solomons around this time to prepare for New Georgia.
'Jap' was the standard, derogatory wartime term for Japanese people and things. Kept as written.

1943-06-11_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
the boat for
the Officer's Club

1943-06-11_tom-to-mother.txt.note: The formal announcement of John and Fran's engagement.
By mid-June 1943 LCI Flotilla Five had moved up to the Guadalcanal area, where the coconut plantations were a familiar sight, to prepare for the New Georgia landings three weeks later.

1943-06-11_tom-to-mother.txt.text: by the news from Washington and London
1943-06-11_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Probably Churchill's visit to Washington (the Trident Conference, May 1943) and his May 19 speech to Congress promising offensives against Japan.

1943-08-01_tom-to-mother.txt.note: There are no letters between June 11 and Aug. 1, 1943. During those weeks LCI(L)-62 took part in the New Georgia landings (battle credit July 1 and 4, 1943), which Tom could not mention under censorship.
Headaches and fever were among the first signs of malaria, which was rife in the Solomons; Tom was hospitalized with malaria in 1945.

1943-08-19_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom teases Isabel, who had apparently joined the WAVES.

1943-08-19_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
single bars come in both gold and
silver

1943-08-24_tom-to-mom.txt.note: John's bachelor party before his wedding to Fran.
Unidentified, perhaps a nickname for an uncle or a family pet.

1943-08-24_tom-to-mom.txt.text: travel allowance from Norfolk to Houston
1943-08-24_tom-to-mom.txt.note: Officers were reimbursed for travel under orders, but had to turn in their orders to claim it.

1943-08-31_tom-to-mother.txt.note: About $31,000 in today's money, carried ashore in cash.
Men returning from a long overseas tour could expect about 30 days' leave.

1943-09-05_tom-to-mom.txt.text: The boys are finally in Europe

The Japs are beginning to believe it is worthwhile to shoot
and run
1943-09-05_tom-to-mom.txt.note: Uses the wartime slur 'Japs'. In context: after losing Munda (Aug. 5), the Japanese were pulling back through the central Solomons, and the Allies bypassed Kolombangara by landing on Vella Lavella (Aug. 15, 1943).

1943-09-05_tom-to-mom.txt.text:
Contrary to
Public Opinion the Japs are smart
1943-09-05_tom-to-mom.txt.note: Wartime propaganda often portrayed the Japanese as inferior. Men in combat areas knew better.
The envelope itself was not scanned.

1943-09-15_tom-to-mother-sweetheart.txt.note: A playful greeting to his mother; the letter answers her Ocean City letter and mentions her birthday party.

1943-09-23_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Mail was sometimes lost when ships or planes carrying it went down.
Army units in the Solomons staged shows, and touring USO troupes visited the larger bases.
A rare luxury at forward bases, and a famous morale booster. Small ships had no ice-cream machines.

1943-10-02_tom-to-mom.txt.text:
John & George inherited their
poker sense from Dad
1943-10-02_tom-to-mom.txt.note: This line confirms that John and George are Tom's brothers.

1943-10-09_tom-to-john-and-fran.txt.text: can't use either rugs or curtains
1943-10-09_tom-to-john-and-fran.txt.note: Wartime shortages: textile mills were making military goods, and furnishings were hard to buy.

1943-10-09_tom-to-john-and-fran.txt.text:
pessimistic
about the oil future to be building a coal cellar
1943-10-09_tom-to-john-and-fran.txt.note: With heating oil rationed, many families converted back to coal. The joke has an edge for an oil-business family.

1943-11-27_tom-to-mum.txt.note: Tom's joke for a poker game, timed for payday.

1943-11-27_tom-to-mum.txt.text:
not
eaten under the best circumstances
1943-11-27_tom-to-mum.txt.note: Perhaps a hint of operations: in late Nov. 1943 LCIs were running reinforcements to the Bougainville beachhead.

1943-12-06_tom-to-mum.txt.note: A Chicora resident or business used as a landmark; not identified.

The planned length of a South Pacific tour for small-craft officers. In fact Tom came home after about 13 months, in spring 1944.
Apparently bad news about someone named Jack that Glenn Scott's family had kept from him, perhaps a casualty. Not identified.
Not identified. Frazier is Tom's middle name, so perhaps relatives or a family firm.

1943-12-17_tom-to-mother.txt.text:
When Dad's picture arrived I had
such a strange sensation
1943-12-17_tom-to-mother.txt.note: One of the clearest signs that Tom's father had died, probably in Dec. 1942 or Jan. 1943.

1943-12-25_tom-to-olive-and-bob-pelkey.t.note: The Pelkeys' note, which gives Tom's mother's first name.

1944-01-04_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Servicemen numbered their letters so the family could tell whether any had been lost or arrived out of order.

One year since leaving the States (February 1943).

1944-02-20_tom-to-mum.txt.text: the European Front except that it isn't easy going
1944-02-20_tom-to-mum.txt.note: In Feb. 1944 the Allies were stalled at Anzio and Monte Cassino in Italy.

1944-04-03_tom-to-mum.txt.note: Tom may already have left LCI(L)-62 and been in transit home. He was back in the U.S. by spring 1944, while the ship stayed in the Pacific.

1944-11-02_tom-to-mother.txt.note: Tom was waiting for orders, possibly back to sea (he had expected a second Pacific tour).

1945-03-15_tom-to-mother-portland.txt.note: For Tom's car, a Chevrolet (see the typed winter 1945 letter). Gasoline was still rationed.

Probably Newark, N.J., on her way to the West Coast and then overseas.

1945-05-08_tom-to-mum-ve-day.txt.text:
A week ago it was sunk with
very few survivors
1945-05-08_tom-to-mum-ve-day.txt.note: Almost certainly USS Eagle 56, torpedoed off Portland on April 23, 1945. Officially it was blamed on a boiler explosion, which may be why Tom 'wants to know more about it'.

1945-05-23_tom-to-mom-hospital.txt.note: Probably the yellow skin caused by Atabrine, the anti-malaria drug.

1945-winter_tom-to-mother-typed-portland.note: Released Dec. 1944, which helps date this undated letter to winter 1944-45.

1945-winter_tom-to-mother-typed-portland.text:
ANY DUTY
IN THE STATES IS GOOD DUTY
1945-winter_tom-to-mother-typed-portland.note: A common feeling among men who had served overseas.

undated_bill-jameson-to-mrs-beck.txt.note: Army enlisted men could apply for Officer Candidate School or the Army Air Forces cadet program.

undated_dad-to-tommy-wednesday.txt.note: Not identified. In the late 1930s the oil industry faced several federal and state antitrust inquiries. Dad's summons suggests he was an oil producer or company officer.

undated_daddy-to-tommy-hotel-st-george.t.text: Most of the caddies are dirty looking foreigners
undated_daddy-to-tommy-hotel-st-george.t.note: A prejudiced remark about immigrant caddies, typical of nativist attitudes of the 1920s-30s. Kept as written.
Probably young Tommy's newspaper route, though it could mean schoolwork.

undated_janny-to-mother-pcw.txt.note: Probably the Seventh Avenue Hotel in downtown Pittsburgh.
Women's colleges paired each freshman with an upperclass 'big sister'.
Home Economics, a popular course of study for women.

undated_mother-to-folks-moore-heights.tx.note: Probably a bridge club. 'Cavendish' was a common name for bridge clubs, after the famous London and New York clubs, and she mentions her score out of 16.
The only letter in the collection written by Tom's mother.
